title: Work, institutions and formal letters
objectives: I can address someone formally in speech and in writing, with 'па́не' or 'па́ні' and the vocative of a first name or a surname, or with the first name and patronymic in the vocative.

I can write a short formal letter or email: a greeting with 'Шано́вний' or 'Шано́вна', 'Ви' with a capital letter, a request with 'Прошу́' or 'Про́симо' and an infinitive, and the closing 'З пова́гою'.
I can fill in an application, 'зая́ва', and ask an institution for a certificate, 'до́відка'.
I can talk about a job, an interview, a salary and my experience, and use 'коле́га' for a man or for a woman.
I can form nouns in '-ння' from verbs, and explain how 'резюме́', 'співбе́сіда' and 'з пова́гою' are written and said.

vocabulary.note: Genitive 'роботода́вця': the 'е' of '-ець' drops when an ending is added, as in 'кана́дець', 'кана́дця'. It joins 'робо́та', work, and the root of 'дава́ти', to give, with '-ець', the suffix that names a person: the one who gives the work.

example.source: The employer asked me for my résumé.

vocabulary.note: Genitive 'співробі́тника'. Feminine 'співробі́тниця'. The prefix 'спів-' means 'together with', and 'робітни́к' is a worker, from 'робо́та'; the two words are stressed differently. It is the usual word for a member of staff of an office, a company or an institution.

example.source: Our institution has a hundred employees.

vocabulary.note: One form for a man and for a woman; the words that agree with it show which: 'мій коле́га' for a man, 'моя́ коле́га' for a woman. It declines like 'кни́га' whoever it names, so the dative and locative are 'коле́зі'.

example.target: Це моя́ коле́га Со́фія, а це мій коле́га Тара́с.
example.source: This is my colleague Sofiia, and this is my colleague Taras.

vocabulary.note: A shortening of 'заробі́тна пла́та', earned pay. It is the everyday word for what a job pays, and in Ukraine it is counted by the month.

example.source: What is the salary in this position?

vocabulary.note: A job as a place in an organization, named by its title: 'поса́да вчи́теля', the position of teacher. You work 'на поса́ді', with 'на' and the locative, as with 'на робо́ті'.

example.source: He works as an engineer.

vocabulary.note: A loan word that never changes form, like 'кафе́': 'моє́ резюме́', 'у резюме́', 'два резюме́'.

example.source: Have you read my résumé?

vocabulary.note: Built from 'спів-', together with, and 'бе́сіда', a conversation. It names a job interview or an admission interview. You go 'на співбе́сіду' and you are 'на співбе́сіді'.

example.source: I have a job interview tomorrow.

vocabulary.note: A written request to an institution or an employer, in a fixed form that opens with 'Прошу́' and ends with the date and a signature. You write it ('писа́ти') or fill it in ('запо́внити').

example.source: Please write an application.

vocabulary.note: A short official paper in which an institution confirms a fact: that you study or work there, what you earn, that you were ill. 'До́відка з мі́сця навча́ння', literally 'certificate from place of-study', confirms where you study.

example.source: Where can I get a certificate?

vocabulary.note: A public or official organization: a university, a hospital, a bank, a state office. The 'у' at its start belongs to the word and never changes.

example.target: У цій устано́ві працю́ють до шо́стої.
example.source: This office is open until six.
example.source_literal: In this institution they-work until sixth.

vocabulary.note: Genitive 'докуме́нта', with '-а' as for a concrete countable thing. A passport and a certificate are documents. 'Принести́', to bring, is 'нести́' with the prefix 'при-'.

example.source: Which documents do I need to bring?

vocabulary.note: Genitive 'пі́дпису'. It is built from 'під', under, and the root of 'писа́ти': a signature is written under a text.

example.source: Your signature is missing here.

vocabulary.note: 'Підпишу́', 'підпи́шеш', 'підпи́шуть': 'с' becomes 'ш' in every form of the perfective future, as in the present of 'писа́ти'. The imperfective partner is 'підпи́сувати' ('підпи́сую').

example.source: Please sign here.

vocabulary.note: 'Запо́вню', 'запо́вниш', second conjugation. It is built on 'по́вний', full. The imperative is 'запо́вни', 'запо́вніть': the stem ends in two consonants, so it keeps '-и' and '-іть' although the stem is stressed. The imperfective partner is 'запо́внювати' ('запо́внюю').

example.source: I have already filled in the application.

vocabulary.note: 'Звільню́ся', 'зві́льнишся', 'зві́льняться'; the imperfective partner is 'звільня́тися'. It is built on 'ві́льний', free: to free oneself from a job, 'звільни́тися з робо́ти'. Without '-ся', 'звільни́ти' means to dismiss: 'Його́ звільни́ли.' (They fired him.)

example.source: Why did you quit?

vocabulary.note: Genitive 'до́свіду'. It means skill and knowledge gained by doing something: 'до́свід робо́ти', work experience. It does not name a single event you have lived through.

example.target: У ме́не є до́свід робо́ти вчи́телем.
example.source: I have experience working as a teacher.
example.source_literal: At me is experience of-work by-teacher.

vocabulary.note: It opens a formal letter and agrees with the person addressed: 'Шано́вний па́не...', 'Шано́вна па́ні...', 'Шано́вні коле́ги!'. A letter to a friend or a relative opens with 'Дороги́й' or 'Дорога́' instead.

example.target: Шано́вні коле́ги, дя́кую за ва́шу робо́ту!
example.source: Dear colleagues, thank you for your work!
example.source_literal: Respected colleagues, I-thank for your work!

vocabulary.note: Genitive 'листа́', plural 'листи́': the stress moves to the ending in every other form. It names a paper letter and an email alike. 'Лист' also means a leaf, as in 'листопа́д', November, literally 'leaf-fall'.

example.source: I wrote a letter to Ms. Sofiia.

vocabulary.note: The usual closing of a formal letter, followed by a comma and the writer's name on the next line. It is 'з' with the instrumental of 'пова́га', respect.

example.source: Yours sincerely, Oksana Kovalenko

vocabulary.note: A form asks for it first: 'прі́звище, ім’я́, по ба́тькові', surname, first name, patronymic. 'По ба́тькові', literally 'by father', names the patronymic.

example.source: What is your surname?

dialogues.title: A job interview
dialogues.context: Sam has answered an advertisement from the company, 'компа́нія', where Taras works: it is looking for a teacher of English for its staff. Sofiia, Taras's manager, interviews him. They have just met, so they say 'ви', and she addresses him as 'па́не Се́ме'. 'Зру́чно' is a predicative word made from 'зру́чний', convenient: 'Мені́ зру́чно.' means 'It suits me.'

lines.speaker: Со́фія
lines.target: До́брий день, па́не Се́ме! Я Со́фія. Ду́же приє́мно.
lines.source: Hello, Mr. Sam! I'm Sofiia. Nice to meet you.
lines.source_literal: Good day, sir Sam! I Sofiia. Very pleasant.

lines.speaker: Сем
lines.target: До́брий день, па́ні Со́фіє! Мені́ теж ду́же приє́мно. Дя́кую, що запроси́ли мене́ на співбе́сіду.
lines.source: Hello, Ms. Sofiia! Nice to meet you too. Thank you for inviting me to the interview.
lines.source_literal: Good day, madam Sofiia! To-me also very pleasant. I-thank, that you-invited me to interview.

lines.speaker: Со́фія
lines.target: Я прочита́ла ваш лист і резюме́. Ви вже рік працю́єте вчи́телем англі́йської мо́ви, пра́вда?
lines.source: I've read your letter and your résumé. You've been working as an English teacher for a year, haven't you?
lines.source_literal: I read your letter and résumé. You already year work by-teacher of-English of-language, truth?

lines.speaker: Сем
lines.target: Так. А до цього́ я працюва́в офіціа́нтом у Кана́ді.
lines.source: Yes. And before that I worked as a waiter in Canada.
lines.source_literal: Yes. And before this I worked by-waiter in Canada.

lines.speaker: Со́фія
lines.target: Чому́ ви хо́чете працюва́ти в на́шій компа́нії?
lines.source: Why do you want to work at our company?

lines.speaker: Сем
lines.target: Мій друг Тара́с, ваш коле́га, ка́же, що тут ціка́ва робо́та й до́брі лю́ди.
lines.source: My friend Taras, your colleague, says that the work here is interesting and the people are nice.
lines.source_literal: My friend Taras, your colleague, says, that here interesting work and good people.

lines.speaker: Со́фія
lines.target: Це пра́вда. На́ші співробі́тники щодня́ пи́шуть листи́ коле́гам з і́нших краї́н, і ми хо́чемо, щоб вони́ писа́ли без поми́лок.
lines.source: That's true. Our staff write letters to colleagues in other countries every day, and we want them to write without mistakes.
lines.source_literal: This truth. Our employees every-day write letters to-colleagues from other countries, and we want, so-that they wrote without mistakes.

lines.speaker: Сем
lines.target: Я мо́жу допомогти́. Ми бу́демо чита́ти ї́хні листи́ ра́зом, і я поясню́ ко́жну поми́лку.
lines.source: I can help. We'll read their letters together, and I'll explain every mistake.
lines.source_literal: I can to-help. We will to-read their letters together, and I will-explain each mistake.

lines.speaker: Со́фія
lines.target: До́бре. Зарпла́та на цій поса́ді бу́де два́дцять ти́сяч гри́вень на мі́сяць, а ро́зклад зру́чний: чоти́ри дні на ти́ждень.
lines.source: Good. The salary in this position will be twenty thousand hryvnias a month, and the schedule is convenient: four days a week.
lines.source_literal: Good. Salary on this position will-be twenty thousand of-hryvnias on month, and schedule convenient: four days on week.

lines.speaker: Сем
lines.target: Мені́ зру́чно. А хто працюва́в на цій поса́ді до ме́не?
lines.source: That suits me. And who had this position before me?
lines.source_literal: To-me convenient. And who worked on this position before me?

lines.speaker: Со́фія
lines.target: На́ша коле́га О́ля. Вона́ звільни́лася, бо переї́хала до Льво́ва.
lines.source: Our colleague Olia. She quit because she moved to Lviv.
lines.source_literal: Our colleague Olia. She freed-self, because moved to Lviv.

lines.speaker: Сем
lines.target: А коли́ я мо́жу поча́ти?
lines.source: And when can I start?

lines.speaker: Со́фія
lines.target: Прийді́ть, будь ла́ска, за́втра. Ви запо́вните зая́ву, а в понеді́лок уже́ почнете́ працюва́ти.
lines.source: Please come tomorrow. You'll fill in an application, and on Monday you'll already start work.
lines.source_literal: Come, be kindness, tomorrow. You will-fill-in application, and on Monday already will-start to-work.

lines.speaker: Сем
lines.target: Дя́кую, па́ні Со́фіє! До за́втра.
lines.source: Thank you, Ms. Sofiia! See you tomorrow.
lines.source_literal: I-thank, madam Sofiia! Until tomorrow.

dialogues.title: At the dean's office
dialogues.context: Oksana's summer employer, a museum, has asked her for a certificate from the university saying that she is a student. She has written to the dean's office, 'декана́т', the office of the dean, 'дека́н', who heads a faculty, and now she goes there in person. Bohdan works there; they say 'ви', and she addresses him as 'па́не Богда́не'. 'Па́спорт' means a passport, and 'студе́нтський квито́к', literally 'student ticket', is a student card. 'По ба́тькові', literally 'by father', is the patronymic.

lines.speaker: Окса́на
lines.target: До́брий день! Мене́ зва́ти Окса́на Ковале́нко. Я писа́ла вам про до́відку з мі́сця навча́ння.
lines.source: Hello! My name is Oksana Kovalenko. I wrote to you about a certificate of enrollment.
lines.source_literal: Good day! Me to-call Oksana Kovalenko. I wrote to-you about certificate from place of-study.

lines.speaker: Богда́н
lines.target: До́брий день, па́ні Окса́но. Так, я пам’ята́ю ваш лист. Ви принесли́ па́спорт і студе́нтський квито́к?
lines.source: Hello, Ms. Oksana. Yes, I remember your letter. Have you brought your passport and your student card?
lines.source_literal: Good day, madam Oksana. Yes, I remember your letter. You brought passport and student ticket?

lines.speaker: Окса́на
lines.target: Так, ось вони́.
lines.source: Yes, here they are.
lines.source_literal: Yes, here they.

lines.speaker: Богда́н
lines.target: Дя́кую. Тепе́р запо́вніть, будь ла́ска, зая́ву. Споча́тку напиші́ть прі́звище, ім’я́ й по ба́тькові.
lines.source: Thank you. Now please fill in the application. First write your surname, first name and patronymic.
lines.source_literal: I-thank. Now fill-in, be kindness, application. First write surname, name and by father.

lines.speaker: Окса́на
lines.target: А що писа́ти пі́сля сло́ва «Прошу́»?
lines.source: And what do I write after the word 'Прошу́'?
lines.source_literal: And what to-write after word «I-ask»?

lines.speaker: Богда́н
lines.target: Напиші́ть: «Прошу́ ви́дати мені́ до́відку з мі́сця навча́ння для роботода́вця».
lines.source: Write: 'Please issue me a certificate of enrollment for my employer.'
lines.source_literal: Write: «I-ask to-issue to-me certificate from place of-study for employer».

lines.speaker: Окса́на
lines.target: Ось, я все запо́внила.
lines.source: There, I've filled everything in.
lines.source_literal: Here, I all filled-in.

lines.speaker: Богда́н
lines.target: Ви не написа́ли число́ й не підписа́ли зая́ву.
lines.source: You haven't written the date or signed the application.
lines.source_literal: You not wrote date and not signed application.

lines.speaker: Окса́на
lines.target: Ой, ви́бачте! Ось.
lines.source: Oh, I'm sorry! Here.

lines.speaker: Богда́н
lines.target: Дя́кую. Зая́ву підпи́ше дека́н, а до́відку вам ви́дасть моя́ коле́га, па́ні Мари́на.
lines.source: Thank you. The dean will sign the application, and my colleague, Ms. Maryna, will give you the certificate.
lines.source_literal: I-thank. Application will-sign dean, and certificate to-you will-issue my colleague, madam Maryna.

lines.speaker: Окса́на
lines.target: А коли́ я мо́жу її́ взя́ти?
lines.source: And when can I pick it up?
lines.source_literal: And when I can it to-take?

lines.speaker: Богда́н
lines.target: Че́рез три дні. Прихо́дьте в четве́р пі́сля деся́тої.
lines.source: In three days. Come on Thursday after ten.
lines.source_literal: Through three days. Come on Thursday after tenth.

lines.speaker: Окса́на
lines.target: Дя́кую, па́не Богда́не! До поба́чення.
lines.source: Thank you, Mr. Bohdan! Goodbye.
lines.source_literal: I-thank, sir Bohdan! Until seeing.

lines.speaker: Богда́н
lines.target: До поба́чення, па́ні Окса́но.
lines.source: Goodbye, Ms. Oksana.
lines.source_literal: Until seeing, madam Oksana.

dialogues.title: Checking the letter
dialogues.context: Before he sends his letter to Sofiia, Sam asks his teacher, Iryna Petrivna, to read it. Teacher and student say 'ви' to each other. 'Кли́чний відмі́нок' is the vocative case, and 'з вели́кої лі́тери', literally 'from big letter', means with a capital letter.

lines.speaker: Сем
lines.target: Іри́но Петрі́вно, чи не могли́ б ви прочита́ти мій лист? Я пишу́ до компа́нії, де працю́є Тара́с.
lines.source: Iryna Petrivna, could you read my letter? I'm writing to the company where Taras works.
lines.source_literal: Iryna Petrivna, whether not could would you to-read my letter? I write to company, where works Taras.

lines.speaker: Іри́на Петрі́вна
lines.target: Звича́йно. Кому́ ви пи́шете?
lines.source: Of course. Who are you writing to?
lines.source_literal: Of course. To-whom you write?

lines.speaker: Сем
lines.target: Па́ні Со́фії. Як почина́ють такі́ листи́?
lines.source: To Ms. Sofiia. How do people begin letters like this?
lines.source_literal: To-madam to-Sofiia. How they-begin such letters?

lines.speaker: Іри́на Петрі́вна
lines.target: «Шано́вна па́ні Со́фіє!» Ім’я́ тут у кли́чному відмі́нку.
lines.source: 'Шано́вна па́ні Со́фіє!' The name is in the vocative here.
lines.source_literal: «Respected madam Sofiia!» Name here in vocative case.

lines.speaker: Сем
lines.target: А що ще важли́во?
lines.source: And what else is important?
lines.source_literal: And what still important?

lines.speaker: Іри́на Петрі́вна
lines.target: Коли́ ви пи́шете одні́й люди́ні, «Ви», «Вам» і «Ваш» пи́шуть з вели́кої лі́тери.
lines.source: When you write to one person, 'Ви', 'Вам' and 'Ваш' are written with a capital letter.
lines.source_literal: When you write to-one to-person, «Ви», «Вам» and «Ваш» they-write from big letter.

lines.speaker: Сем
lines.target: А як закі́нчити лист?
lines.source: And how do I end the letter?
lines.source_literal: And how to-finish letter?

lines.speaker: Іри́на Петрі́вна
lines.target: Напиші́ть «З пова́гою», а під цим своє́ ім’я́.
lines.source: Write 'З пова́гою', and your name under it.
lines.source_literal: Write «With respect», and under this own name.

lines.speaker: Сем
lines.target: А якби́ я писа́в чолові́кові з прі́звищем Петре́нко?
lines.source: And if I were writing to a man with the surname Petrenko?
lines.source_literal: And if-would I wrote to-man with surname Petrenko?

lines.speaker: Іри́на Петрі́вна
lines.target: Тоді́ «Шано́вний па́не Петре́нку!» А жі́нці з таки́м прі́звищем пи́шуть «Шано́вна па́ні Петре́нко!»
lines.source: Then 'Шано́вний па́не Петре́нку!' And to a woman with that surname they write 'Шано́вна па́ні Петре́нко!'
lines.source_literal: Then «Respected sir Petrenko!» And to-woman with such surname they-write «Respected madam Petrenko!»

lines.speaker: Сем
lines.target: А жіно́че прі́звище Петре́нко завжди́ таке́ са́ме?
lines.source: And the woman's surname Petrenko always stays the same?
lines.source_literal: And feminine surname Petrenko always such same?

lines.speaker: Іри́на Петрі́вна
lines.target: Так, у ко́жному відмі́нку.
lines.source: Yes, in every case.

lines.speaker: Сем
lines.target: Ду́же дя́кую! Тепе́р я зна́ю, як писа́ти таки́й лист.
lines.source: Thank you very much! Now I know how to write a letter like this.
lines.source_literal: Very I-thank! Now I know, how to-write such letter.

grammar.title: Formal address: 'ви', 'Ви' in letters, and 'па́не' and 'па́ні' with the vocative
grammar.explanation:
Formal address rests on three things you already know: the pronoun 'ви', the nouns 'пан' and 'па́ні', and the vocative case. This note adds the capital 'Ви' of letters, surnames, and the adjective that opens a formal letter.

In speech you say 'ви' at work to one person you do not know well, to anyone older or senior, to an official and to every customer, and to any group. At a job interview both sides say 'ви'. Colleagues of the same age often move to 'ти', and in many IT companies everyone does, but a first meeting starts with 'ви'.

In writing, a letter or an email to one person writes 'Ви' with a capital letter as a mark of respect, and with it every form of the pronoun and of the possessive 'ваш':

- 'Ви', 'Вас', 'Вам', 'Ва́ми', 'на Вас'
- 'Ваш', 'Ва́ша', 'Ва́ше', 'Ва́ші' and their other forms

A letter to several people writes 'ви' with a small letter, and so does every other text, such as a dialogue in a book. The capital belongs to writing only; it is not heard.

To address someone formally, put 'па́не', the vocative of 'пан', before a man's name, and 'па́ні', which never changes, before a woman's name. The name itself is in the vocative:

- a first name, the usual choice at work: 'па́не Богда́не', 'па́ні Со́фіє'
- a surname, in letters and in official settings: 'па́не Петре́нку', 'па́ні Ковале́нко'
- or, without 'па́не' and 'па́ні', the first name and the patronymic, both in the vocative: 'Іри́но Петрі́вно', 'Іва́не Петро́вичу'

The word for a surname is 'прі́звище'. The most common Ukrainian surnames end in '-енко' ('Петре́нко', 'Ковале́нко', 'Шевче́нко'), and they behave differently for men and for women. A man's surname in '-енко' is a masculine noun in '-о' and declines like 'та́то': as 'та́то' has the vocative 'та́ту', 'Петре́нко' has 'па́не Петре́нку'. Its other cases are regular too: 'для па́на Петре́нка', 'па́нові Петре́нкові', 'з па́ном Петре́нком'. A woman's surname in '-енко', like a woman's surname that ends in a consonant ('Ткачу́к'), never changes, in the vocative or in any other case: 'па́ні Ковале́нко', 'для па́ні Ковале́нко', 'з па́ні Ткачу́к'.

A formal letter opens with the adjective 'шано́вний', respected, before the name. It agrees with the person: 'Шано́вний' for a man, 'Шано́вна' for a woman, 'Шано́вні' for several people ('Шано́вні коле́ги!'). Ukrainian adjectives have no vocative form of their own, so 'шано́вний' keeps the nominative while the nouns after it take the vocative: 'Шано́вний па́не Петре́нку!', literally 'respected sir Petrenko!'. English opens such a letter with 'Dear'; Ukrainian keeps 'Дороги́й' and 'Дорога́' for letters to friends and family ('Дорога́ Окса́но!').

rows: '-е' for the name, '-у' for the patronymic

grammar.title: The formal letter and the application: 'Прошу́', 'Про́симо' and 'З пова́гою'
grammar.explanation:
A formal letter or email follows a fixed order, and a Ukrainian reader notices when a part is missing:

- the greeting, on its own line and with an exclamation mark: 'Шано́вна па́ні Ковале́нко!' (in emails a comma is also common)
- the text, which starts on the next line with a capital letter and says at once why you write: 'Пишу́ Вам про...', 'Пишу́ Вам, бо...'
- the request
- a line of thanks or of waiting for an answer: 'Дя́кую.', 'Чека́ю на Ва́шу ві́дповідь.'
- the closing 'З пова́гою' with a comma, and the writer's name, usually the full name, on the line below

The request is the heart of the letter, and its usual form is 'Прошу́' with an infinitive. 'Прошу́' is the 'я' form of 'проси́ти', to ask for, so 'Прошу́ ви́дати мені́ до́відку.' is literally 'I-ask to-issue to-me certificate': 'Please issue me a certificate.' An organization writing in its own name uses the 'ми' form, 'Про́симо', 'we-ask': 'Про́симо запо́внити зая́ву.' The stress moves: 'прошу́' is stressed on the ending, 'про́сиш' and 'про́симо' on the stem. The person asked, when named, is in the accusative ('Прошу́ вас підписа́ти...'), and the person something is done for is in the dative ('ви́дати мені́').

The infinitive after 'Прошу́' is usually perfective, because a letter asks for one act with a result: 'ви́дати', 'підписа́ти', 'запо́внити'. An imperfective infinitive asks for something repeated or ongoing: 'Про́симо прихо́дити з па́спортом.' (Please always come with your passport.) In conversation the same request is an imperative with 'будь ла́ска' ('Запо́вніть, будь ла́ска, зая́ву.') or the polite conditional 'Чи не могли́ б ви...?'; 'Прошу́' with an infinitive belongs to writing and to official speech.

An application to an institution or an employer, 'зая́ва', has a layout of its own:

- in the top right corner, the person it is addressed to, in the dative: 'Дека́нові', to the dean; 'Дире́кторові', to the director
- below that, the sender, with 'від' and the genitive: 'від студе́нтки Окса́ни Ковале́нко'
- in the middle, the word 'Зая́ва'
- the request, starting with 'Прошу́'
- at the bottom, the date on the left and the signature on the right

Two applications every working person meets use fixed words. To be hired: 'Прошу́ прийня́ти мене́ на поса́ду вчи́теля.', where 'прийня́ти' means to accept, to take on. To resign: 'Прошу́ звільни́ти мене́ з поса́ди за вла́сним бажа́нням.', literally 'I-ask to-release me from post by own wish'. 'Вла́сний', own, is related to 'вла́сник', owner, and 'бажа́ння', wish, is a noun made from 'бажа́ти' by the rule of the next note.

examples.target: Прошу́ ви́дати мені́ до́відку з мі́сця робо́ти.

grammar.title: Nouns of work: 'коле́га' and the nouns in '-ння'
grammar.explanation:
Two kinds of noun run through the language of work.

The first is the noun of common gender: a noun with one form for a man and for a woman, whose gender in a sentence is the sex of the person it names. 'Коле́га', colleague, is the one you will use most. It ends in '-а' and declines like 'кни́га' whoever it names, but every word that agrees with it, the possessive, the adjective and the past form of the verb, is masculine for a man and feminine for a woman:

- 'Мій коле́га прийшо́в.' (My colleague came: a man.)
- 'Моя́ коле́га прийшла́.' (My colleague came: a woman.)
- 'Я дзвоню́ своє́му коле́зі.' and 'Я дзвоню́ свої́й коле́зі.' (I am calling my colleague.)
- 'з на́шим коле́гою' and 'з на́шою коле́гою' (with our colleague)

Keep it apart from two other kinds of noun in '-а'. 'Мико́ла' is a masculine noun: it always names a man and always takes masculine agreement. 'Люди́на' and 'дити́на' are feminine nouns used for anyone: 'Моя́ дити́на хво́ра.' is said of a son as well as of a daughter, and the agreement stays feminine. Only a noun of common gender changes its agreement with the person. Many words for people at work have two separate forms instead, one for each sex: 'співробі́тник' and 'співробі́тниця', 'вчи́тель' and 'вчи́телька'. 'Коле́га' itself serves for both, with agreement that follows the person, and that is what makes it a noun of common gender.

The second is the verbal noun: a neuter noun that names an action as a thing, as English 'signing' or 'completion' does. Official Ukrainian uses verbal nouns much more than everyday speech, and almost all of them end in '-ння', with a doubled 'н', or in '-ття'. You have met several: 'пита́ння', question; 'оголо́шення', advertisement; 'повідо́млення', message; 'закі́нчення', ending. They are built from the infinitive by a regular rule:

- a verb in '-ати' or '-яти', '-ува́ти' included, drops '-ти' and adds '-ння': 'чита́ти', 'чита́ння'; 'підписа́ти', 'підписа́ння'; 'бажа́ти', 'бажа́ння'; 'планува́ти', 'планува́ння'; 'навча́тися', to study, 'навча́ння', with '-ся' left out
- most verbs in '-ити' replace it with '-ення', with the consonant change of its passive participle in '-ений': 'запо́внити', 'запо́внення'; 'закі́нчити', 'закі́нчення'; 'повідо́мити', 'повідо́млення', as 'зро́блений' has 'бл'; 'запроси́ти', 'запро́шення', invitation, as 'прошу́' has 'ш'
- a few verbs with a short stem take '-ття', as their participle takes '-тий': 'відкри́ти', 'відкриття́', opening or discovery; 'прийня́ти', 'прийняття́'; 'життя́' stands to 'жи́ти' in the same way
- a verb in '-іти' keeps its 'і': 'розумі́ти', 'розумі́ння', understanding

The stress often stays where the infinitive has it ('запо́внити', 'запо́внення'), but not always ('запроси́ти', 'запро́шення'), so learn it with each noun. These nouns are neuter and decline like 'життя́': the genitive is the same as the nominative ('для запо́внення', for filling in), the instrumental ends in '-ям' ('з бажа́нням', willingly, literally 'with wish'), and the locative in '-і' ('у запро́шенні', in the invitation). The nominative plural is also the same, and the genitive plural has a single 'н', a soft sign and no ending: 'пита́ння', 'пита́нь'.

Where official text writes a verbal noun, speech prefers a verb. A notice says 'Пі́сля підписа́ння докуме́нта...' (after the signing of the document), and a colleague says 'Коли́ ви підпи́шете докуме́нт...' (when you sign the document). Both are correct; choose the noun when you write formally.

grammar.title: Spelling and sound: резюме́, співбе́сіда, з пова́гою and the other new words
grammar.explanation:
Most of the new words are read with the rules of the alphabet units. Three of them need a closer look.

'Резюме́' is a loan word, and like 'кафе́' and 'меню́' it is neuter and never changes form: 'моє́ резюме́', 'у резюме́', 'два резюме́'. Its stress is on the last syllable. The 'р' is hard before 'е', the 'з' is soft before 'ю', and the 'м' is hard before 'е': [rɛzʲuˈmɛ]. The unstressed 'е' of the first syllable leans a little toward 'и', as unstressed 'е' always does.

'Співбе́сіда' is built from the prefix 'спів-', together with, and 'бе́сіда', a conversation. The 'в' of 'спів-' ends its syllable before a consonant, so it is said [w], as in 'Петрі́вна': [spʲiwˈbɛsʲidɑ]. The same prefix and the same [w] are in 'співробі́тник' [spʲiwrɔˈbʲitnɪk]. The 'п' is slightly softened before 'і', like every consonant there, and 'с' and 'д' are soft before 'і'.

In 'з пова́гою' the preposition is 'з', the default form, because it opens the phrase before a single consonant; 'із' and 'зі' appear only where the euphony rules call for them. It has no stress of its own and is said together with the next word, as if the two were one word with one stress. 'Пова́гою' is the instrumental of 'пова́га', with '-ою' after a hard stem, and its 'г' is the voiced [ɦ] of 'голова́': [pɔˈʋɑɦɔju].

The other new words show patterns you have met:

- 'роботода́вець', 'роботода́вця': the 'е' of '-ець' drops when an ending is added, as in 'кана́дець', 'кана́дця'. The compound has one stress, on 'да', and the 'о' after 'робот-' only links its two parts.
- 'коле́га', 'коле́зі': 'г' becomes 'з' before the ending '-і', as in 'кни́га', 'у кни́зі'.
- 'до́відка', 'у до́відці': 'к' becomes 'ц' before '-і', as in 'апте́ка', 'в апте́ці'.
- 'підписа́ти', 'підпишу́', 'підпи́шеш': 'с' becomes 'ш' in every form of the perfective future, as in the present 'пишу́' of 'писа́ти'.
- 'пі́дпис', 'пі́дпису': the stress is on the prefix, while 'підписа́ти' is stressed on the ending; learn each word with its own stress.
- 'лист', 'листа́', 'листи́': one syllable in the nominative singular, and the stress on the ending in every other form.
- 'запо́внити', 'шано́вний': 'в' before 'н' ends its syllable and is said [w]: [zɑˈpɔwnɪtɪ], [ʃɑˈnɔwnɪj].
- 'звільни́тися': the soft sign makes the 'л' soft before 'н', as in 'ві́льний'. The stress is on the ending in 'звільню́ся' and on the stem in 'зві́льнишся', whose '-шся' is said [sʲːɑ].
- 'зая́ва': 'я' after the vowel 'а' is [jɑ]: [zɑˈjɑʋɑ].
- 'прийня́ти': 'й' closes the first syllable, and 'я' after 'н' makes the 'н' soft: [prɪjˈnʲɑtɪ].
- 'запо́внення', 'підписа́ння': the doubled 'нн' before 'я' is one long soft [nʲː], as the doubled 'тт' of 'життя́' is: [zɑˈpɔwnɛnʲːɑ]. The participle 'запо́внений' has a single 'н', so the letters tell the two words apart.
- 'прі́звище': 'зв' is two sounds, [zʋ], and 'щ' is [ʃt͡ʃ], as in 'що'.

culture.title: Documents, applications and the manners of the office
culture.text:
Ukrainian institutions run on documents, on paper and more and more on screens. A visit to a university office, a bank or a state office usually means an application, 'зая́ва', in the fixed layout of this unit, a certificate, 'до́відка', that confirms a fact, and a signature on every page that matters. Two documents are asked for most often:

- the passport, 'па́спорт', which since 2016 has been issued as a plastic ID card
- the tax number, a ten-digit number that every resident receives

Students also carry a student card, 'студе́нтський квито́к', literally 'student ticket'. Since 2020 the state app 'Ді́я' keeps digital copies of these documents on a phone, and many services can be used in it without any paper at all. Its name means 'action', and it also reads as 'Держа́ва і я', 'the state and I'.

Forms ask for a name in a fixed order: 'прі́звище, ім’я́, по ба́тькові', surname, first name, patronymic. The patronymic, literally 'by father', is made from the father's first name: the daughter of a man named 'Петро́' has the patronymic 'Петрі́вна', and his son 'Петро́вич'. Official papers use all three parts, and in schools, hospitals and state offices a senior colleague is often addressed by first name and patronymic, as Sam addresses his teacher: 'Іри́но Петрі́вно'.

Workplaces differ in their manners. Banks, schools, hospitals and state offices keep 'ви' and formal address, while many IT companies use first names and 'ти' from the first day, even with managers. A job interview still begins with 'ви', and it is the senior person who suggests moving to 'ти'. A résumé, 'резюме́', usually fits on one or two pages, and a short cover letter, with 'Шано́вний' or 'Шано́вна', 'Ви' with a capital letter and 'З пова́гою', is the polite way to send it.

paragraphs.target: Компа́нія, в які́й працю́ють дві́сті програмі́стів, запро́шує на поса́ду вчи́теля англі́йської мо́ви.
paragraphs.source: A company with two hundred programmers is hiring a teacher of English.
paragraphs.source_literal: Company, in which work two-hundred of-programmers, invites to position of-teacher of-English of-language.

paragraphs.target: На́ші співробі́тники щодня́ пи́шуть листи́ коле́гам з і́нших краї́н, і ми хо́чемо, щоб вони́ говори́ли й писа́ли англі́йською без поми́лок.
paragraphs.source: Our staff write letters to colleagues in other countries every day, and we want them to speak and write English without mistakes.
paragraphs.source_literal: Our employees every-day write letters to-colleagues from other countries, and we want, so-that they spoke and wrote by-English without mistakes.

paragraphs.target: Ми запро́шуємо люди́ну, яка́ гово́рить англі́йською з дити́нства й ма́є до́свід робо́ти вчи́телем. Ми пропону́ємо до́бру зарпла́ту, зру́чний ро́зклад і ціка́ву робо́ту з молоди́ми коле́гами.
paragraphs.source: We are looking for someone who has spoken English since childhood and has experience as a teacher. We offer a good salary, a convenient schedule and interesting work with young colleagues.
paragraphs.source_literal: We invite person, who speaks by-English from childhood and has experience of-work by-teacher. We offer good salary, convenient schedule and interesting work with young colleagues.

paragraphs.target: Про́симо до п’я́тниці написа́ти лист Со́фії й дода́ти до ньо́го резюме́. Співбе́сіди бу́дуть у понеді́лок і вівто́рок.

paragraphs.target: Ваш коле́га Тара́с, мій друг, сказа́в мені́, що у Вас ціка́ва робо́та. Я хоті́в би працюва́ти з Ва́шими співробі́тниками й допомага́ти їм писа́ти без поми́лок.

paragraphs.source_literal: Application will-sign dean, and certificate to-You they-will-issue through three days.

paragraphs.target: Декана́т працю́є з понеді́лка до п’я́тниці, з дев’я́тої ра́нку до шо́стої ве́чора. З пе́ршої до дру́гої годи́ни в нас пере́рва на обі́д.
paragraphs.source: The dean's office is open from Monday to Friday, from nine in the morning to six in the evening. From one to two o'clock we have a lunch break.
paragraphs.source_literal: Dean's-office works from Monday until Friday, from ninth of-morning until sixth of-evening. From first until second of-hour at us break for lunch.

paragraphs.target: Якщо́ у Вас є пита́ння, напиші́ть нам у ві́дповідь на цей лист.
paragraphs.source: If you have any questions, write to us in reply to this letter.
paragraphs.source_literal: If at You is question, write to-us in answer on this letter.

questions.prompt: What must Oksana bring to the dean's office?
choices: Her passport and her student card
questions.explanation: 'Про́симо принести́ з собо́ю па́спорт і студе́нтський квито́к.'
'Зая́ву підпи́ше дека́н': the dean will sign it. Bohdan signs only the letter.

questions.prompt: When is the dean's office closed on a weekday?
choices: From nine to ten in the morning
questions.explanation: 'З пе́ршої до дру́гої годи́ни в нас пере́рва на обі́д': the lunch break is from one to two.

questions.prompt: How should Oksana ask a question about the certificate?
choices: By writing a reply to the letter
By asking the dean at home
questions.explanation: 'Напиші́ть нам у ві́дповідь на цей лист' asks her to reply to the letter.

exercises.prompt: Match the Ukrainian words with their meanings
Match the words for documents and forms with their meanings
Which phrase closes a formal letter?
exercises.explanation: 'З пова́гою', literally 'with respect', comes before the writer's name. 'Бува́й' is a goodbye to a friend, and 'На добра́ніч' is said at bedtime.

exercises.prompt: What does 'роботода́вець' say word for word?
exercises.explanation: It joins 'робо́та', work, and the root of 'дава́ти', to give, with '-ець', the suffix that names a person. A co-worker is 'співробі́тник'.

exercises.prompt: How do you say 'my colleague' about a woman?
exercises.explanation: 'Коле́га' is a noun of common gender: the possessive is feminine for a woman, 'моя́', and masculine for a man, 'мій'. 'Мої́ коле́ги' is the plural.

exercises.audio_target: У п’я́тницю в ме́не співбе́сіда в ба́нку.
choices: On Friday I have a job interview at a bank.
On Friday I have a job interview at a museum.
On Monday I have a job interview at a bank.

exercises.prompt: You write a formal letter to Mr. Petrenko. Which greeting do you use?
exercises.explanation: For a man, 'шано́вний' is masculine, 'пан' is in the vocative, 'па́не', and his surname in '-енко' takes '-у'. 'Шано́вна па́ні Петре́нко!' greets a woman, and 'Дорога́ Окса́но!' a friend.

exercises.prompt: In which text is 'Ви' written with a capital letter?
choices: A letter to one person whom you address formally
A letter to a group of colleagues
A dialogue between two people in a story
exercises.explanation: The capital is a mark of respect in a letter to one person. A letter to several people and ordinary text write 'ви'.

exercises.prompt: Why does the surname stay the same in 'Шано́вна па́ні Ковале́нко!'?
choices: A woman's surname in '-енко' never changes.
'Па́ні' puts the next word in the nominative.
exercises.explanation: A woman's surname in '-енко' has one form in every case. A man's surname in '-енко' does change: 'па́не Ковале́нку'.
A man's surname in '-енко' declines like 'та́то', so its vocative ends in '-у', as 'та́ту' does.

choices: My colleague got married last week.

exercises.prompt: Which word is the noun that names the action of filling in?
exercises.explanation: 'Запо́внити', a verb in '-ити', gives the verbal noun 'запо́внення', with '-ення' and a doubled 'н'. 'Запо́внений', with one 'н', is the passive participle, and 'запо́внити' is the infinitive.

choices: The stress moves to the ending.
The 'е' of '-ець' drops when an ending is added, as in 'кана́дця'.
'Роботода́вець' is a noun of common gender.
exercises.explanation: The 'е' of '-ець' drops when an ending is added: 'кана́дець', 'кана́дця'; 'хло́пець', 'хло́пця'. The stress stays on 'да'.

exercises.prompt: Why does 'резюме́' keep the same form in 'у моє́му резюме́'?
choices: The locative of neuter nouns has no ending.
It is a loan word that never changes form, like 'кафе́'.
exercises.explanation: 'Резюме́', like 'кафе́' and 'меню́', is a neuter loan word with one form for every case and number. The ending of 'моє́му' still shows the locative.

exercises.hint_source: My colleague quit her job yesterday.
exercises.explanation: 'Моя́' shows that the colleague is a woman, so the past form is feminine: 'звільни́лася'. After the vowel '-а' the suffix may also be '-сь'.

exercises.hint_source: Fill in the application and sign it.
Please issue me a certificate of my salary.
exercises.explanation: A formal request is 'Прошу́' with an infinitive, here the perfective 'ви́дати', to issue, since the letter asks for one act.

exercises.prompt: In 'Я написа́в лист своє́му коле́зі', why does 'коле́га' have a 'з'?
choices: Before the ending '-і', 'г' becomes 'з', as in 'у кни́зі'.
exercises.explanation: 'Коле́га' declines like 'кни́га', and 'г' becomes 'з' before '-і' in the dative and the locative: 'коле́зі'.
'Дзвони́ти' takes the dative, and the dative of 'коле́га' is 'коле́зі'. 'Своє́му' is masculine, so the colleague is a man.

exercises.prompt: An organization asks you in writing to sign a document. Which sentence does it write?
exercises.explanation: An organization writing in its own name uses 'Про́симо' with an infinitive. 'Підпиши́!' is an order to a friend, and 'Ми підписа́ли' means 'we signed'.

exercises.hint_source: Thank you for the invitation to the interview!
exercises.explanation: 'Запроси́ти' is a verb in '-ити', so its verbal noun ends in '-ення', with 'с' changed to 'ш' as in 'прошу́': 'запро́шення'. Note that the stress moves to 'про'.

exercises.prompt_target: Чи ма́єте ви ___ робо́ти з дітьми́?
exercises.hint_source: Do you have experience of working with children?
exercises.explanation: 'До́свід робо́ти' is work experience. 'Ма́ти' takes the accusative, which for 'до́свід' is the same as the nominative.

exercises.prompt_source: Our colleague Taras is writing a letter.
Thank you for your reply. (in a letter to one person)

exercises.explanation: 'Звільни́тися' is the perfective reflexive verb 'to quit'. Without '-ся', 'звільни́ти' means to dismiss someone.

exercises.hint_source: Here are my résumé and my letter.

exercises.prompt_source: My colleague (a man) works as an engineer.
answers: Мій коле́га працю́є на поса́ді інжене́ра.
exercises.explanation: The colleague is a man, so the possessive is 'мій'. A job after 'працюва́ти' is in the instrumental: 'інжене́ром'.

exercises.prompt_source: Please sign the application. (to someone you call 'ви')
exercises.explanation: In conversation a request is an imperative with 'будь ла́ска'. The 'я' form 'підпишу́' is stressed on the ending, so the imperative for 'ви' is 'підпиші́ть'.

exercises.prompt_source: I have a job interview on Monday.
exercises.explanation: 'У ме́не співбе́сіда' says what you have at a set time, and 'є' is left out because existence is not the point; 'Я ма́ю співбе́сіду' says the same with 'ма́ти'. Euphony gives 'у' at the start of a sentence and after a consonant, and 'в' after a vowel.

exercises.prompt_source: We ask you to fill in the application. (an organization writing to one person)
exercises.explanation: An organization uses 'Про́симо' with a perfective infinitive. In a letter to one person 'Вас' takes a capital letter, and it may be left out.
